newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says deal on U.N. dues reflects its policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says deal on U.N. dues reflects its policy.

text.p: The U.S. State Department on Friday welcomed passage by a key Senate committee of a bill that would repay most of the U.S. debt to the United Nations and said conditions it sets broadly reflect U.S. policy.

The Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Thursday voted 14-4 for the measure under which the United States would pay $819 million to the world body, which says Washington owes it around $1.3 billion.
To receive the payment, the United Nations would have to implement a string of spending and staff cuts, reduce Washington's annual dues and make other concessions.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright "does consider the action yesterday by the committee to be a major step forward in trying to resolve the long-standing problem we have had".

Agreement on the bill was reached earlier this week after four months of negotiations between the committee's Republican chairman, Jesse Helms of North Carolina, and its leading Democrat, Joseph Biden of Delaware.

Burns said Wednesday that talks were continuing over some details, but he said Friday: "We believe the conditions that the legislation would impose for payment of arrears generally reflect administration policy for UN reform."
The U.S. spokesman forecast "hard-fought negotiations" in the U.N. Secretariat and with other member states before the deal was accepted by the United Nations.
But he said U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan was committed to the idea of reform, and the idea of linking the paying off of U.S. arrears to implementing changes was "appropriate and achievable".
"I don't believe the United States is being onerous here, or impossible in our demands," Burns told a news briefing.

"The fact is that we are the largest donor, and the American taxpayers have a right, as well as certainly the members of the Senate and the House, to expect that the administration will be vigorous in supporting the concept of reform," he added.
